content: Quality Assurance in Study Processes To ensure high-quality work throughout all stages of the study, specific measures will be implemented. These measures will cover the collection of data and specimens in the field, as well as their subsequent processing and analysis. Study Limitations All potential biases that could influence the study results must be identified and listed. Safety and Monitoring An adverse event is defined as any unfavorable and unintended sign (including abnormal laboratory findings), symptom, or disease that occurs in temporal association with a protocol-specified procedure, regardless of whether it is considered related to the procedure itself. Normal physiological changes that do not significantly deviate in frequency or severity from expected levels are not classified as adverse events. A serious adverse event (SAE) refers to an adverse event that results in death, is life-threatening, causes persistent or significant disability/incapacity, necessitates inpatient hospitalization or prolongs an existing hospitalization, leads to a congenital anomaly or birth defect, or is associated with cancer or overdose. Additionally, device malfunctions or failures that could directly or indirectly result in serious medical consequences, such as death or significant health deterioration, are also considered SAEs. However, for a biomarker survey, the risk of SAEs is minimal, as the only procedure involved is blood specimen collection. Use of Dried Blood Spot (DBS) Specimens Currently, no in vitro diagnostic tests have been validated by manufacturers for use with DBS specimens, nor have they received regulatory approval for such use. Therefore, the use of DBS specimens is considered off-label. Linkage to Care The framework for the study will be adapted to align with the local healthcare system. The organization of pre-counseling, counseling, and treatment for patients who test positive will be clearly described. Protection of Human Subjects Community Engagement and Follow-Up The study team will engage with the community to prepare the field for the study and ensure that results are communicated back to the community. Risks and Inconveniences to Participants The study will outline the potential experiences participants may face during data collection. Measures to ensure the confidentiality of interviews and the anonymity of collected information will be detailed. Benefits to Participants The study will explain how laboratory results will be communicated to participants and how those who test positive will benefit from their participation by being offered appropriate treatment. Informed Consent A separate assent form with simplified language will be prepared for children. This form will allow them to provide assent for participation in the questionnaire and blood collection. An example of such a form is provided in Appendix 2 of the protocol template. Expected Benefits of the Survey This section will outline the individual and public health benefits derived from the survey. It will also include plans to use the results to guide public health actions. Budget The total budget for the survey will include field costs, in vitro diagnostics, and treatment for individuals who test positive. The source of funding for all components of the budget must be identified. In countries where national health insurance covers treatment, the survey budget can indicate that treatment will be supported by the national health insurance system. Specimen Types and Processing Requirements Venous Whole Blood Use the specimen immediately after collection. Fresh whole blood collected via venepuncture should be processed promptly. Serum Collect whole blood, mix gently by hand 4–5 times, and allow it to clot. The serum fraction should be separated from the clotted red blood cells. Process within 30 minutes of collection. Store at 2–8°C and test within 5 days or as specified by the assay instructions. Plasma Collect whole blood, mix gently by hand 8–10 times, and centrifuge for up to 10 minutes. Plasma should be separated after centrifugation. Process within 6 hours of collection. Store at 2–8°C and test within 5 days or as specified by the assay instructions. Capillary Whole Blood Use the specimen immediately, following the instructions for the recommended specimen transfer device. Capillary blood is collected via finger-stick using a lancet and transfer device. Oral Fluid Use the specimen immediately, following the instructions for the recommended collection device. Oral mucosal transudate (not saliva) is collected from the gums using a collection device. Dried Blood Spot (DBS) Store at 4°C for up to 3 months or at –20°C for longer periods. Whole blood (venous or capillary) is applied to filter paper and later eluted for testing. The use of specific assays with DBS must be validated by the manufacturer. If not validated, the use of DBS is considered off-label and unauthorized for returning medical results. References The references include key guidelines and position papers from WHO, UNAIDS, and other authoritative sources on hepatitis and HIV testing, survey methodologies, and best practices for specimen handling and processing.
